name: W25Q32JVZPIQ
title: 3 V 32M-bit serial flash memory with dual and quad SPI
summary: W25Q32JV is a 32M-bit (4M-byte) serial flash memory on a single 2.7 V to 3.6 V supply, reached over standard, dual or quad SPI at up to 133 MHz. Its 256-byte pages program in one go and erase in 4KB sectors, 32KB or 64KB blocks or as a whole chip, with suspend and resume. Protection comes from status register bits, the /WP pin or per-block locks; it also holds three 256-byte OTP-lockable security registers, a 64-bit unique ID and an SFDP table. It comes in 8-pin SOIC, VSOP, PDIP, WSON and XSON, 16-pin SOIC and 24-ball TFBGA packages, for -40 °C to +85 °C or +105 °C.
key_figures: 133 MHz (3.0 V to 3.6 V), 104 MHz (2.7 V to 3.0 V); Read Data 03h 50 MHz
SPI modes 0 and 3; dual and quad output and I/O
4KB sector 45 ms typ; 64KB block 150 ms typ; chip 10 s typ
100,000 program-erase cycles min per sector; over 20 years

notes: All parts are 32M-bit (4M-byte), 2.7 V to 3.6 V (code V).

Order code: W, 25Q (SpiFlash with 4KB sectors and dual/quad I/O), 32J (32M-bit), V (2.7 V to 3.6 V), two-letter package code, temperature grade I (industrial, -40 °C to +85 °C) or J (industrial plus, -40 °C to +105 °C), then Q or M.

Q and M are both green packages: lead-free, RoHS compliant, halogen-free (TBBA) and free of antimony oxide (Sb2O3). Q parts have QE fixed at 1, so /HOLD is off and standard, dual and quad I/O work with no setup; they are backward compatible with the FV family. M parts have QE = 0 and programmable, and carry a new device ID that marks the JV family.

The top-side marking leaves off the W prefix and uses only the second letter of the package code (N, S, T, F, A, B, C); ZP and ZE parts carry no package letter, and XG parts are marked Q32JVXG followed by the grade and option letters.
Bulk parts ship in tubes (shape E); tape and reel (shape T) or tray (shape S) are ordered as an option.

operation.text: 32M-bit, 4M-byte array in 16,384 pages of 256 bytes. One program operation writes 1 to 256 bytes. Erase works on a 4KB sector (16 pages), a 32KB block (128 pages), a 64KB block (256 pages) or the whole chip: 1,024 sectors and 64 blocks. Beside the array sit a 256-byte SFDP register, three 256-byte security registers and a 64-bit unique ID.

Standard SPI uses CLK, /CS, DI and DO; dual SPI turns DI and DO into IO0 and IO1; quad SPI adds IO2 and IO3. SPI modes 0 and 3 are both accepted; they differ only in whether CLK idles low (mode 0) or high (mode 3) while /CS changes. Inputs are taken on rising CLK edges and outputs change on falling edges. At 133 MHz the dual and quad reads give 266 MHz and 532 MHz equivalent rates, up to 66 MB/s of continuous data.

Quad instructions (6Bh, EBh, 32h, 94h) need QE = 1 in Status Register-2. With QE = 1, /WP becomes IO2 and /HOLD (or /RESET on the 8-pin parts) becomes IO3, and the hold function is gone. IM/JM parts leave the factory with QE = 0 and allow it to be written; IQ/JQ parts have QE fixed at 1.

With /CS high the part is deselected: data outputs are high impedance and the supply current falls to standby unless an internal erase, program or status write is still running. Taking /CS low selects it and raises the current to the active level. After power-up, /CS has to go from high to low before the first instruction is taken. /CS should follow VCC as it rises and falls; a pull-up resistor on /CS does this.

While /CS is low, pulling /HOLD low pauses the device: DO floats and DI and CLK are ignored. Releasing /HOLD lets the transfer carry on. It is meant for sharing the SPI lines among several devices, and it does not exist when QE = 1.

/WP, active low, works with SRP to stop status register writes; together with the CMP, SEC, TB and BP bits it can hardware-protect anything from one 4KB sector to the whole array. /WP must be valid tWHSL before /CS falls and held tSHWL after /CS rises for a status register write.

SOIC-16 and TFBGA parts have a dedicated /RESET input that outranks /CS, CLK and the IOs. Holding it low for at least about 1 µs (tRESET) stops any operation in progress and returns the part to its power-on state. Pulses of a few hundred ns often work, but 1 µs is the recommended minimum. On SOIC-16 the pin has an internal pull-up and may float when unused; elsewhere it may float or be tied to VCC.

Enable Reset (66h) followed straight away by Reset Device (99h) resets the part; any other instruction between the two cancels the enable. Reset takes about 30 µs (tRST), during which nothing is accepted. All volatile settings are lost: volatile status bits, WEL, suspend state, the continuous read mode bits and the wrap setting. An erase or program that is running or suspended at that moment may leave corrupt data, so BUSY and SUS should be read first.

Below VWI the part holds itself in reset and ignores every instruction. Once VCC passes VWI, write enable, program, erase and status write instructions stay locked out for tPUW more; reads are allowed tVSL after VCC reaches its minimum. The part always starts write-disabled with WEL = 0.

An instruction starts when /CS falls; the first byte on DI is the opcode, sent MSB first and sampled on rising CLK edges, and it ends when /CS rises. Opcode, address, dummy and data bytes follow as the instruction tables show. A read may be ended after any bit, but a write, program or erase must end on a byte boundary or it is dropped. While a program, erase or status write runs, only Read Status Register (and Suspend during an erase or program) is accepted.

BUSY (S0) reads 1 during page program, quad page program, any erase, a status register write, or a security register erase or program, and returns to 0 when the cycle is done. WEL (S1) is set by Write Enable (06h) and cleared by power-up, Write Disable and the end of any program, erase, status write or security register operation. Read Status Register (05h, 35h, 15h) works at any time, can be read over and over in one instruction, and is the way to poll BUSY.

With WPS = 0, BP2-BP0 choose how much of the array is read-only, TB picks top (0) or bottom (1), SEC picks 64KB blocks (0) or 4KB sectors (1), and CMP = 1 inverts the selection so the rest of the array is protected instead. All of these are non-volatile and leave the factory at 0.

SRP and SRL decide who may write the status registers: by software after Write Enable (both 0), by /WP when SRP = 1, or not at all until power is cycled when SRL = 1. A one-time-program lock is available as a special order.

LB3-LB1 are one-time-programmable bits, 0 from the factory. Setting one to 1 makes its 256-byte security register permanently read-only; erase and program instructions to that register are then ignored.

With WPS = 1 the BP scheme is ignored and each block has its own lock bit: one for each of the 62 middle 64KB blocks and one for each 4KB sector of the top and bottom blocks (32 sectors). A lock bit of 1 blocks erase and program there. The bits are volatile and all come up as 1 at power-up or after reset, so the whole array starts protected. 36h plus an address locks one block or sector, 39h unlocks it, 3Dh reads its bit back (LSB 1 = locked), 7Eh locks all and 98h unlocks all; 36h, 39h, 7Eh and 98h each need Write Enable first.

Write Enable for Volatile Status Register (50h) before 01h, 31h or 11h writes the bits as volatile values: WEL is not set, BUSY stays 0, the new values take effect within tSHSL2, and the non-volatile copy is untouched and returns at the next power cycle or reset. This avoids the tW write time and wear on the non-volatile bits. SRL and LB3-LB1 cannot be taken from 1 back to 0 this way. A non-volatile write (06h then 01h, 31h or 11h) runs for tW with BUSY = 1.

For compatibility with earlier Winbond parts, 01h followed by two data bytes writes Status Register-1 and -2; /CS must rise after the sixteenth data bit. If /CS rises after eight bits only Status Register-1 changes and Status Register-2 is left as it was (older parts cleared CMP and QE in that case).

03h and a 24-bit address return data on DO from that address onward; the address counts up after every byte, so one instruction can read the whole array. The clock may run from D.C. to fR (50 MHz). Issued while BUSY = 1 it is ignored and the running cycle is unaffected.

Fast Read (0Bh), Fast Read Dual Output (3Bh) and Fast Read Quad Output (6Bh) add eight dummy clocks after the address so the clock can run up to FR. Data comes out on one, two or four pins; for 3Bh and 6Bh the IO pins must be released to high impedance before the falling edge of the first data clock.

Fast Read Dual I/O (BBh) takes the address two bits per clock and Fast Read Quad I/O (EBh) four bits per clock, cutting the overhead of random access for execute-in-place. Each is followed by a mode byte M7-M0, to be set to Fxh; EBh then needs four dummy clocks before data. EBh needs QE = 1.

Set Burst with Wrap (77h) followed by 24 dummy bits and the wrap byte sets W6-W4 for every following EBh read. With W4 = 0 the output wraps inside an 8, 16, 32 or 64-byte section of the 256-byte page, starting at the given address, until /CS rises: a cache can fetch the critical word first and fill the line. Another 77h with W4 = 1 returns to normal reads.

After Write Enable, 02h, a 24-bit address and 1 to 256 data bytes program erased (FFh) locations; /CS stays low for the whole instruction and must rise right after the eighth bit of a byte, or nothing is programmed. A full page should start at an address with A7-A0 = 0. Bytes past a page boundary wrap to its first byte; fewer than 256 bytes leave the other bytes of that page untouched as long as they do not run past its end. Programming lasts tPP with BUSY = 1, then WEL clears. A page protected by the BP bits or a lock bit is not programmed.
32h works as 02h but takes data on IO0-IO3; it needs QE = 1 and Write Enable. The gain is for programmers and systems with clocks below about 5 MHz; at higher clock rates programming time dominates.

After Write Enable, 20h (4KB sector), 52h (32KB block) or D8h (64KB block) with a 24-bit address, or C7h/60h for the whole chip, sets the region to FFh. /CS must rise on a byte boundary. The erase lasts tSE, tBE1, tBE2 or tCE with BUSY = 1 and then clears WEL. A protected region is not erased; chip erase does nothing if any region is protected.

operation.topic: Erase and program suspend and resume
operation.text: 75h, accepted only with SUS = 0 and BUSY = 1 while a sector erase, block erase or page program runs, pauses it within tSUS: BUSY drops to 0 and SUS goes to 1, and other sectors or blocks can then be read (or, during an erase suspend, programmed). During erase suspend, 01h and the erase instructions (20h, 52h, D8h, C7h, 60h, 44h) are refused; during program suspend, 01h and the program instructions (02h, 32h, 42h) are refused. Chip erase cannot be suspended. 7Ah, accepted only with SUS = 1 and BUSY = 0, clears SUS at once and sets BUSY again within 200 ns. Suspend must not follow a resume by less than tSUS. Losing power while suspended resets SUS and may corrupt data in that page, sector or block; a resume after that is ignored.

B9h, with /CS raised after the eighth bit, puts the part into power-down within tDP. There only ABh is recognised, not even Read Status Register, which makes power-down a strong write protection. ABh alone brings the part back after tRES1, with /CS held high meanwhile; ABh with three dummy bytes also returns the 8-bit device ID and the part is ready tRES2 after /CS rises. ABh is ignored while BUSY = 1. The part always powers up in standby, not in power-down.

90h with address 000000h returns the manufacturer ID EFh then the device ID; 92h and 94h do the same with the address and data on two or four pins (94h has four dummy clocks first, and both need M7-M0 = Fxh), and the two IDs repeat alternately while clocked. 9Fh returns the JEDEC ID: EFh, the memory type byte and the capacity byte. 4Bh and four dummy bytes return the factory-set 64-bit unique ID.

5Ah, a 24-bit address with A23-A8 = 0 and A7-A0 as the start byte, then eight dummy clocks, reads the 256-byte SFDP register, which follows JESD216. Its contents are defined in Winbond's SFDP application note.

Three 256-byte security registers sit apart from the main array. 44h erases one in tSE, 42h programs 1 to 256 bytes of one, both after Write Enable; 48h reads with eight dummy clocks at up to FR, the byte address wrapping from FFh back to 00h within the register. A register whose LB bit is set can no longer be erased or programmed.
133 MHz (FR) needs VCC from 3.0 V to 3.6 V; from 2.7 V to 3.0 V the limit is 104 MHz. Read Data (03h) is limited to 50 MHz across the range.
At least 100,000 program-erase cycles per sector and more than 20 years of data retention.
The metal pad under the WSON packages has no internal connection; it may be left floating or joined to GND. Exposed PCB vias under the pad are to be avoided.
The TFBGA balls have a 0.45 mm land and 0.35 mm opening; a PCB ball land of 0.35 mm or less is suggested.
